$comment: Per-body lens profiles. Data, not code: two cameras are in use and a third
will not need a patch, just an entry.
Matched against the footage itself - `layout` is how the body stores its two
lenses (the X1 writes one stream per file, _00_ and _10_ side by side; the X4
puts both in one file as two streams) and `frame` is the square lens frame's
pixel size. Between them they identify the body without trusting a filename.
ih_fov/iv_fov MUST both exceed 180 or the two lenses cannot meet and every
seam-crossing shot renders a black wedge - checkLens() enforces this.
`circle` is how far the image circle reaches as a fraction of the inscribed
radius, measured off real frames: the X4's is exactly inscribed (1.00) while
the X1's overfills its frame and is still lit past the edge (1.05). It sets
the seam mask, so getting it wrong either trims real picture or blends dead

`denoise` is the body's default grain reduction, applied after the warp and BEFORE the colour block so the grade never amplifies what it removes. luma/chroma are hqdn3d spatial strengths (temporal derived at 1.2x). Chroma is nearly free and luma is not - see denoiseChain() for the measured table. A shot overrides with its own `denoise`, or opts out with {"enabled": false}.

x1.label: Insta360 ONE X
x1.notes: 190 measured by mapping both lenses into one equirect and sweeping for best overlap agreement; clean unimodal peak across two independent moments. circle left at 1.0 (conservative): frames are still lit to ~1.05, so this trims a little real picture at the very rim rather than risking dead corners in the blend.

denoise.notes: Not measured on this body - the X4 figure is fitted to X4 footage and a different sensor and bitrate is a different noise floor. Left at zero rather than inherited, so nobody reads an untested number as a measurement. Run the hood-anchor comparison on real X1 footage before filling this in.

x4.label: Insta360 X4
x4.notes: NOT a physical calibration, and deliberately so - 194/181 is the framing Ian aimed and signed off on for the in-cabin shots (2026-08-06), because the near-181 vertical is what makes the interior stop looking domed. The glass is round: the lit image circle on a real X4 frame measures round to within 0.1% (sigma x/y = 1.0004 and 1.0007 on the cleanly-lit lens), so a vertical field 13 degrees under the horizontal is an anamorphic squeeze layered on the projection, not a measurement. It is a look, kept because it looks right. Two things follow. iv_fov must stay ABOVE 180 - checkLens rejects anything at or below and silently substitutes the fallback, so a saved 180 would render at 190/190 with only a printed note. And the seam mask must stay ROUND (see circleMaskExpr): deriving it from the two fields made it an ellipse, which at these values tore a 663-pixel uncovered strip across the top of frame; round, the same aim gets 3464 pixels of overlap and no gap. The physical field is nearer 196.5 - that was measured against an Insta360 Studio export of the same clip and moment, used as geometric ground truth. Studio's Dewarp is documented as RECTILINEAR (onlinemanual.insta360.com), and a projection sweep agreed: rectilinear scored 0.66 against stereographic 0.34. With projection pinned to rectilinear, sweeping ih_fov gives a clean unimodal peak at 196-197 (0.667), falling smoothly either side - the first trustworthy number this body has had. Earlier self-consistency attempts all failed because the only X4 footage is in-cabin, so the whole seam ring is within a metre of the lenses and parallax swamps the signal; matching an external reference sidesteps that entirely. CAVEAT: this is the value that makes our ideal equisolid model best imitate Studio's output. If Studio applies a per-model lens profile on top, 196.5 absorbs some of that rather than being the bare physical field - which is what we want for matching them, but is not the same claim. Ian had set 193 by eye, which was close.

denoise.notes: Measured on ian-west-run-3 forward, Solo Nationals 2026, anchored on Fergus's painted hood - a smooth surface, so all high-frequency detail there is noise. chroma 10 removes 39% of the chroma speckle for -8% luma noise and +2% edge detail: it does not touch luma at all, so the small detail gain is measurement noise rather than a real sharpening. luma left at 0 deliberately - every luma setting tested cost about one unit of real detail per 1.2 units of noise, which is a per-shot call, not a default. What reads as 'grainy' on this body is the colour speckle, and this is the part of it that is free.
